name: Dice Poker
intro: A short path through Dice Poker: the hand rankings, then which dice to keep for your second roll and when to stand.

units.name: How Dice Poker works
units.blurb: Two rolls and the hand rankings.

lessons.title: The hand rankings
lessons.summary: Dice Poker hands run from nothing up to five of a kind. Learn the rankings, including why a full house beats a straight, and spot hands in a roll.
lessons.wrap: Nine hands, best to worst: five, four, full house, high straight, low straight, three, two pair, pair, nothing. Next: a quick rules check.

steps.text:
You and your opponent each roll five dice. After your first roll, keep any dice you like and roll the rest once more, or stand. The best poker hand wins the round; first to three rounds wins.

From best to worst: five of a kind, four of a kind, full house, high straight (2–6), low straight (1–5), three of a kind, two pair, one pair, nothing.

steps.prompt: Tap the dice that make this hand.
steps.wrong: Look for matching numbers. There are two sets.

steps.explain: 1 to 5 is a low straight. 2 to 6 is a high straight.

steps.prompt: Which is better: a full house or a high straight?
steps.explain: A full house, even though straights are slightly rarer in one roll. That’s the traditional order from card poker. When two hands are the same type, the higher numbers win.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Five questions on the rules. Pass to unlock the strategy.

lessons.title: Dice Poker rules check
lessons.summary: Test your Dice Poker rules: rolls per turn, reading a hand, the order of hands and how ties between the same hand are broken.
lessons.wrap: Rules check passed. Now for the strategy.

steps.prompt: Tap the dice that make this hand.
steps.wrong: Four dice show the same number.

steps.prompt: How many times can you roll in one turn?
steps.explain: Your first roll and one reroll of any dice you choose.

steps.prompt: You have three 5s, your opponent has three 6s. Who wins?
steps.explain: Same hand type, so the higher numbers win.

steps.prompt: Which ranks higher: a low straight or a high straight?

units.name: Keeping and standing
units.blurb: Which dice to keep, and when to stop.

lessons.title: What to keep
lessons.summary: Your one reroll decides most rounds of Dice Poker. Learn what to keep with three of a kind, two pair, one pair and an almost-straight.
lessons.wrap: Keep the sets, roll the rest. Next: when to stand.

steps.text: With three of a kind, keep them and roll two dice for four of a kind or a full house.
steps.done: Keep the three 5s and roll two.

steps.text: With two pair, keep both pairs and roll one die for a full house.
steps.done: One die to roll: a 4 or a 6 makes a full house.

steps.text: Here you have a pair of 5s, and also 2, 3, 4, 5: four in a row.
steps.wrong: Chasing the straight needs one exact die. The pair gives you three dice to improve with.
steps.done: Keep the pair and roll three. Four to a straight only works if one die lands on the number you need: a 1 in 3 chance at best. Chase it only if a straight is what you need to win.

steps.explain: Keep the highest die, or roll all five.

lessons.title: When to stand
lessons.summary: In Dice Poker you can stand instead of rerolling. Learn when to stop: as soon as you’re winning if you roll second, and on a full house if you roll first.
lessons.wrap: Stand when you’re winning, or on a full house when you go first. The same idea of knowing when to stop helps in Five Dice and Ship, Captain and Crew.

position.label: Your first roll. Opponent: two pair

steps.text: If you roll second, you know what you have to beat.
steps.prompt: Your opponent stood on two pair. You have three 4s. Reroll or stand?
steps.explain: Stand. Three 4s already beat two pair, so the round is yours. There’s nothing to gain from another roll.

position.label: Your first roll. You go first

steps.text: If you roll first, you don’t know the target yet.
steps.prompt: You have a full house. Reroll or stand?
options: Reroll the 6s for four of a kind
steps.explain: Stand on a full house or better when you go first. Breaking it up usually leaves you with less.

steps.prompt: Your opponent has three 5s. You have a pair of 2s. What now?
steps.explain: You’re losing, so you have to roll. Keep the pair and roll three for a better hand.
